10000.question_text: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
10000.instructions:
The passage given below is followed by a set of questions. Choose the most appropriate answer to each question.

‘Shifting baseline syndrome’ names the process by which ongoing damage to the natural world is normalized over time, as each generation measures loss against an already diminished benchmark. Someone born in the 1970s may recall car windscreens spattered with insects after long journeys. Today’s windscreens bear only a fraction of those marks; yet a person born in the early 2000s would not register this as evidence of drastic ecological decline, having never known the earlier abundance. Also called ‘generational amnesia’, the effect is a powerful force, disguising degradation and enabling its continuation.

This syndrome has masked the steady ruin of rivers. Clean rivers have become rivers you cannot drink from without falling ill, which in turn have become rivers you cannot swim in without risk. Almost too late, we have woken to the scale of the catastrophe. As the river defender Feargal Sharkey has put it, ‘The simple truth of the matter is that every river in England is dying.’ They are dying through neglect, and being killed by design.

Yet decline need not be the only trajectory. Shifting baseline syndrome can operate in reverse. We might normalize recovery as readily as deterioration, and then come to desire its increase: a ‘lifting baseline syndrome’. We can run the reel backwards, imagining a future in which children expect rivers to run clear and free.

Rivers, though easily wounded, possess a remarkable capacity for self-healing when given the chance. Their life returns swiftly. When the Lower Elwha Dam in Washington State was removed in September 2011, a century after its construction, the river’s revival was breathtaking. Vast stores of sediment, long trapped behind the dam, were released to the estuary, where new flows built shingle banks and sandbars, buffering the coast and creating habitats. In the drained reservoir bed, life surged back: saplings of maple, fir and cedar; swathes of lupin; willow and cottonwood. Black bears and mountain lions moved through the regrowth. Dippers appeared, bobbing on boulders like attentive waiters.

Below the surface, further transformations unfolded. As the waters cleared and the river ran unimpeded, migrating salmon returned—first in hundreds, then thousands—driven upstream to spawn and die in the ancient cycle of the salmon run, as strange and compelling as any Greek tragedy.

With the salmon came the wider web of life. Ocean creatures by nature, they carried marine nutrients inland. Their carcasses, dragged into forests by scavengers, were broken down by fungi and absorbed into the soil, nourishing trees. By way of the river, the ocean fed the forest.

People, too, returned: hikers, families, paddlers, policymakers, and members of the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, whose sacred land had long been submerged. Having fought for decades to remove the dams, they scattered native seeds across the recovering terrain. Through such acts, the river was not only restored, but reimagined. Hope, it turns out, is the thing with rivers.
10000.solution:
Answer: 1

Option 1: Correct.
The passage begins by defining “‘Shifting baseline syndrome’” as the process by which “ongoing damage to the natural world is normalized over time.” It emphasizes that this effect is “a powerful force, disguising degradation and enabling its continuation.” However, the author then pivots: “Yet decline need not be the only trajectory. Shifting baseline syndrome can operate in reverse… a ‘lifting baseline syndrome’.” The Elwha example functions as illustration of this possibility. Thus, the central purpose is both diagnostic (explaining normalized decline) and aspirational (proposing normalized recovery).

Option 2: Incorrect.
While the Elwha River restoration is described in rich detail—“the river’s revival was breathtaking,” “life surged back,” and “migrating salmon returned”—this episode occupies only part of the passage and serves as supporting illustration. It exemplifies the broader conceptual shift toward a “lifting baseline syndrome,” rather than constituting the passage’s primary purpose.

Option 3: Incorrect.
The passage briefly notes that rivers are “dying through neglect, and being killed by design,” and quotes Feargal Sharkey: “every river in England is dying.” However, this criticism is contextual, not central. The author’s main thrust is not policy critique but a conceptual reframing of environmental perception and possibility.

Option 4: Incorrect.
Although rivers are said to possess “a remarkable capacity for self-healing when given the chance,” the phrase “when given the chance” implies that human action (e.g., dam removal, seed scattering) is necessary to enable recovery. The passage does not argue that intervention is unnecessary; rather, it shows restoration occurring through deliberate human efforts.

The correct answer is 1

Hence, [1].
options: Explain how generational amnesia conceals environmental decline while proposing that ecological recovery can become similarly normalized and desired.
Document the ecological revival of the Elwha River following dam removal as evidence of nature’s resilience.
Criticize governmental neglect and deliberate policy failures that have led to the degradation of England’s rivers.
Argue that rivers possess an inherent capacity for self-healing that makes human intervention largely unnecessary.

10004.question_text: The author's attitude towards Carl Menger is that of:
10004.instructions:
The passage given below is followed by a set of questions. Choose the most appropriate answer to each question.

Carl Menger's account of the origin of money is deeply satisfying because it shows how money can develop from barter without anyone consciously inventing it. As such, it's a great example of Adam Smith's 'Invisible Hand', or what scientists now call 'emergence'.

 Menger (1840-1921) founded the Austrian school of economics, a heterodox school of thought derided by many mainstream economists. Yet their accounts of the origin of money beg the very question Menger answered. The typical mainstream-economics textbook lists the problems of barter exchange and then explains how money overcomes these problems. However, that doesn't really explain how money actually got started, any more than listing the advantages of air travel explains how airplanes were invented. One is left with the impression that barterers, one morning, suddenly became alert to the benefits of monetary exchange, and, by that afternoon, were busy using some good as money.

That, of course, is ridiculous. In Menger's account, money emerges through a series of small steps, each of which is based on self-interested choices by individual traders with limited knowledge. First, individual barterers realize that when direct exchange is difficult, they can get what they want by indirect exchange. Rather than finding someone who both has what I want and wants what I have, I need only find someone who wants what I have. I can then trade what I have for his good, even though I don't want to consume it myself, and then trade that for something I do want to consume. In that case, I will have used the intermediate good as a medium of exchange.

Menger notes that not all goods are equally marketable; some goods are easier to trade than others. It therefore pays a trader to accumulate an inventory of highly marketable items for use as media of exchange. Other alert traders in the market catch on, and eventually the market converges on a single common medium of exchange. This is money.
10004.solution: While the author's attitude towards Carl Menger is clearly positive, 'elation' (great joy or pride) and 'exultation' (triumphant joy) are too extreme. There is no hint of 'adulation' (excessive devotion or servile flattery) on the author's part. The author's attitude is that of 'admiration' for Carl Menger and his logical account of the origin of money. Hence, [4].

10008.question_text: The passage describes the strong force as:
10008.instructions:
The passage below is accompanied by a set of questions. Choose the best answer to each question.

 

Protons and neutrons, collectively known as nucleons, have less energy per nucleon in helium than in hydrogen, in carbon compared with helium, and so on up to iron. If nuclei overcome their mutual repulsion, they fuse and release energy. The strong nuclear force, more powerful than the electric force but with a very short range, holds them together. Fusion happens only when nuclei get extremely close, which occurs under the intense density and high temperatures inside stars. Once close, they fuse eagerly, releasing vast amounts of energy that power the stars. The strong force is the most powerful of the four fundamental forces. Another, the weak force, plays a role in nuclear reactions, while electromagnetism and gravity are more familiar from daily life. Despite its everyday significance, gravity is the weakest of all. Our weight is the result of Earth's immense mass—about 6 X 1024 kg—pulling on us. It takes the entire planet’s gravity to hold us down with the force we feel.

To grasp how weak gravity is, compare it with electromagnetism, specifically the electric force. Both forces obey an inverse square law, meaning that as distance increases, the force weakens by the square of that distance. But at any given distance, the electric repulsion between two protons is 1036 times stronger than their gravitational attraction. On the scale of nuclei and atoms, gravity is negligible. Molecules are bound by electric forces, with no interference from gravity. Electric forces not only repel but also attract, holding electrons and nuclei in atoms and binding atoms into molecules. These forces, acting between only a few atoms, are what keep an apple attached to its stalk, resisting the pull of Earth’s gravity. There is a constant struggle between electric forces trying to hold matter together and gravity trying to pull it apart. When an apple finally becomes heavy enough to fall, Earth's gravity wins—but only because all of Earth's mass is acting on just one apple.

Gravity differs from the electric force in a crucial way. Electric charge comes in two types, positive and negative, which cancel each other out, so atoms and even the Earth as a whole have no net charge. But gravity always adds up; the more atoms an object has, the stronger its gravitational pull. This explains why large objects like the Moon or planets have enough self-gravity to shape themselves into spheres while individual atoms remain intact. When an object grows as massive as the Sun, its self-gravity becomes so intense that it crushes atoms at its core, forcing nuclei close enough for fusion to occur. This fusion process, driven by the balance of nuclear and gravitational forces, is what powers stars. The strength—or weakness—of gravity ultimately determines a star’s size and how quickly it burns through its nuclear fuel, setting the course for its life and eventual death.
10008.solution:
Option 1. Incorrect. While the strong force governs atomic nuclei, its role is not to prevent spontaneous decay. Instead, it binds protons and neutrons together despite their electromagnetic repulsion.

10012.question_text: Which statement best captures the central idea of the passage?
10012.instructions:
The passage below is accompanied by a set of questions. Choose the best answer to each question.

 

Before China adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1912, the Chinese year was based on the moon's cycle, with each month lasting 28 to 29 days. Since 12 such months totaled fewer than the 365 days of the solar year, the Chinese calendar, like other luni-solar systems, required periodic adjustments. While the Julian and Gregorian calendars extended most months to 30 or 31 days to spread the difference evenly, China retained the traditional moon-length month and instead introduced an additional, or ‘intercalary,’ month every 18 months or so.

Determining when to introduce this extra month was a matter of great concern in ancient China. Proper synchronization of earthly affairs with cosmic rhythms was believed to influence everything—virtue, longevity, prosperity, justice, and immunity from disasters. The responsibility for these essential adjustments—such as setting the year-period, determining seasonal rites, or fine-tuning the pitch of ritual music—ultimately fell to the emperor. Rulers who successfully managed these tasks were praised, especially those who founded dynasties or achieved great feats. Conversely, bad emperors were often accused of neglecting or manipulating these sacred calculations, leading to disorder.

The idea of periodic adjustments was not limited to the calendar; it extended to dynastic succession itself. Some dynasties endured for centuries, while others lasted only a few turbulent decades, appearing as if they had been inserted to fill a gap or redirect history. The Former Han dynasty had been preceded by the short-lived Qin, which was founded by the First Emperor, and the Later Han followed the brief rule of Wang Mang’s Xin dynasty. Observing this pattern, some historians argued that Qin and Xin were ‘intercalary’ dynasties—temporary but necessary disruptions that restored cosmic harmony. Since Chinese historical thought often likened dynastic change to planetary cycles, this interpretation seemed fitting.

Sima Guang, the 11th-century author of the Zizhi Tongjian, attempted to distinguish between legitimate and intercalary dynasties but found the task impossible. By the post-Han period, the sheer number of ruling houses made such categorization impractical. Yet, the title of his historical work, meaning ‘A Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government,’ suggests that history itself was seen as reflecting cosmic cycles. Dynasties, like planets, were believed to rise and fall, wax and wane, shine and fade. Early rulers in a dynasty were often strong and virtuous, while later ones tended to be weaker and corrupt. This cycle was so deeply ingrained in Chinese historical writing that the trope of the ‘bad-last emperor’ became almost a literary convention. These final rulers were often depicted as decadent, irresponsible, or cruel, their reigns marked by scandal and decline. However, these portrayals should be approached with caution, as they often served political narratives rather than objective history. Thus, whether in calendar adjustments or dynastic transitions, Chinese history was deeply influenced by the idea of cycles—of correction, renewal, and inevitable decline—mirroring the movements of the heavens themselves.
10012.solution:
Option 1. Incorrect. While the passage mentions China's adoption of the Gregorian calendar, it does not frame this as the central theme. The discussion is more about traditional Chinese conceptions of time and history rather than a shift to scientific accuracy.

Option 2. Incorrect. The passage explicitly connects the idea of periodic adjustments not only to timekeeping but also to dynastic transitions, rejecting the notion that intercalary months were a purely practical measure.

Option 3. Correct. The passage emphasizes how both calendar adjustments and dynastic changes were seen as part of cosmic cycles, influencing governance, historical interpretation, and even moral order. The reference to intercalary months and intercalary dynasties reinforces this cyclical perspective.

Option 4. Incorrect. Although Sima Guang struggled to categorize dynasties, this is a secondary point. The passage presents historical classification challenges within the broader framework of cyclical patterns rather than portraying them as purely arbitrary.

Hence, [3].

The intercalary month was merely a practical fix for aligning lunar and solar years.
Chinese timekeeping reflects a belief in cosmic cycles, influencing the calendar and dynastic legitimacy.
Sima Guang's failure to distinguish dynasties exposes the arbitrary nature of Chinese historical classification.

  1. When businesswoman and politician Diane Rwigara wanted to challenge Rwanda’s President Kagame in the presidential election, the electoral commission did not accept her candidacy.
  2. According to the World Economic Forum’s Gender Gap Index, Rwanda ranked 12th out of 146 countries.
  3. It has led to undeniable progress in terms of inclusion, with women at the top levels of government.
  4. Laws on issues like education, gender-based violence, and rural poverty - which matter to women in particular - have been passed.
  5. It pointed to better performances in the fields of political representation and health while noting that areas of employment and economic involvement needed improvement.
10018.solution:
Sentence 1: Rwandan electoral commission did not accept Diane Rwigara’s presidential candidacy. 
Sentence 2: 12th on WEF’s Gender Gap index.
Sentence 3: Inclusion of women at top levels of government.
Sentence 4: Formation of laws that matter to women.
Sentence 5: Better performances in political representation and health 

All the sentences talk about women’s representation in Rwanda. This will be followed by 4 as it lists the results of having women in “top levels of government” as given in 3. 2-5-3-4 is the sequence. So, 1 is the odd sentence. Hence, 1

10024.question_text: Which of the following amounts could D not have earned in any single round?
10024.instructions:
Refer to the data below and answer the questions that follow.

A group of four friends - A, B, C and D found Rs. 20 on a table. They decided to play a game of cards to distribute the amount amongst themselves. A deck of cards was kept face down on the table. The rules of the game were as follows:

  • In each round each player draws one card from the pack.

  • If a single player gets a card of the highest value amongst the four, he picks Rs. 4 from the table.

  • If two players get cards of the highest value, they both pick Rs. 2 from the table.

  • If three players get cards of the highest value, each of them takes Re. 1 from the fourth player (if he doesn’t have the money, he simply owes them the amount and has to pay up as soon as he earns it).

  • If all four players get cards of the same value, no one earns anything.

  • Value of the ace is the highest, followed by king, queen, etc., irrespective of the suit.

Then they proceed to the next round.

At the end of 4 rounds:

a) It was found that each player earned a positive amount of money in the same number of rounds.

b) Considering net earnings across all 4 rounds, D earned more than any other player and B earned less than any other player.

c) The amount of money left on the table was Rs.8.
10024.solution:
i. The amount taken from the table is always 4, an even number & it is distributed as either 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 or 2 + 2 + 0 + 0. Thus amount earned by each individual in 3 out of 4 rounds is even.

ii. In the remaining round the 3 players must have tied at the top spot as the amounts of each player is different. Amount added / subtracted in this scenario is 1 or 3 which are odd numbers. Thus, the amounts they must possess at the end of 4 rounds must be odd.

iii. Also D has highest amount & B has the lowest amount. Thus only 1 combination is possible.

Hence, [2].
